problem: Two hedges dropped: 'were every-day matters enough, no doubt, in society' (modern states it flatly) and 'as I found it for the present inexplicable' (modern: 'since I could not explain it', losing 'for the present', which foreshadows later explanation).
new_text: It was not until I had withdrawn to my own room for the night that I steadily reviewed the tale Mr. Rochester had told me. As he had said, there was probably nothing extraordinary in the story itself: a wealthy Englishman's passion for a French dancer, and her betrayal—these were no doubt everyday matters in society. But there was something decidedly strange in the storm of emotion that had suddenly seized him just as he was expressing contentment with his present mood, and his renewed pleasure in the old hall and its surroundings. I thought about this puzzling moment; but gradually letting it go, since for the present I could not explain it, I turned to considering my master's manner toward me. The trust he had chosen to place in me seemed like a tribute to my discretion, and I regarded and accepted it as such. His behaviour toward me had been steadier for some weeks now than at first. I never seemed to be in his way; he no longer had spells of chilling haughtiness. When he met me unexpectedly, the encounter seemed welcome; he always had a word and sometimes a smile for me. When formally invited to his presence, I was received with a warmth that made me feel I genuinely had the power to entertain him, and that these evening conversations were sought as much for his pleasure as for my benefit.

problem: Source 'at your peril you fetch a candle yet' = don't fetch one yet (or else). Modern 'But at your peril, don't fetch a candle yet' can read as the reverse (peril if you don't fetch it).
new_text: "There! I am up now. But don't fetch a candle yet, at your peril. Wait two minutes until I get into some dry clothes, if any are dry—yes, here is my dressing gown. Now run!"

problem: 'I was not aware any danger or annoyance was to be dreaded' — 'or annoyance' dropped; Jane's pointed understatement to Grace loses a term.
new_text: "Fiend! She wants to know my habits, so she can plan accordingly!" Indignation overwhelmed caution. I replied sharply, "Until now I have often forgotten to fasten the bolt. I did not think it necessary. I was not aware there was any danger or annoyance to be feared at Thornfield Hall. But in future"—and I stressed the words—"I shall take care to make everything secure before I go to sleep."

problem: 'It looked a lovely face enough' — the grudging 'enough' is dropped, making Jane's judgment of her own imagined Blanche unqualified ('It was a lovely face').
new_text: I kept my word. An hour or two was enough to sketch my own portrait in chalk, and in less than two weeks I had completed an ivory miniature of an imaginary Blanche Ingram. It was a lovely enough face, and when set beside the real head in chalk, the contrast was as stark as self-control could wish. I benefited from the exercise: it had kept my head and hands busy, and had given force and fixity to the new impressions I wished to stamp indelibly on my heart.
